# Points {background-color="#007155"}

## Most Location Data Starts as a Table {.smaller}

- A list of clinics, schools, grantee projects, or broadband sites usually arrives as a spreadsheet, not a shapefile
- If it has a **longitude** and a **latitude** column, you're one line away from a map
- `nycflights13::airports` is a good example

```{r}
airports
```

- To R, `lat` and `lon` are just two numeric columns. Nothing here knows it's a location yet.

## From Table to `sf`: `st_as_sf()` {.smaller}

```{r}
airports_sf <- airports |>
  st_as_sf(coords = c("lon", "lat"), crs = 4326)

airports_sf
```

- `coords = c("lon", "lat")` names the x column first, then y. **Longitude is x** (east-west), latitude is y.
- `crs = 4326` says these are plain GPS coordinates (WGS84 CRS)
- The `lat` and `lon` columns are gone. They now live in `geometry`, as POINTs.

## Your First Point Map

```{r}
#| fig-height: 4
#| out-width: "75%"
ggplot(airports_sf) +
  geom_sf(size = 0.5)
```

- It works, but it's every US airport in the list, including Alaska, Hawaii, and a few Pacific islands. We want the NBRC states.

## Keep Only the Points Inside

```{r}
#| error: true
nbrc_states <- c("ME", "NH", "NY", "VT")

state_lines <- states(cb = TRUE) |>
  filter(STUSPS %in% nbrc_states)

airports_ne <- airports_sf |>
  st_filter(state_lines)
```

- `st_filter()` keeps the rows of one layer that touch another layer. Here it fails. Read the last line of the error.

## Layers Must Share a CRS {.smaller}

```{r}
st_crs(airports_sf)$input
st_crs(state_lines)$input
```

- Last week's warning, in action: GPS points come in WGS84 (4326), and Census boundaries come in NAD83 (4269)
- Fix it with `st_transform()`, which moves one layer into the other's CRS

```{r}
airports_ne <- airports_sf |>
  st_transform(st_crs(state_lines)) |>
  st_filter(state_lines)

nrow(airports_ne)
```

- `ggplot()` will quietly line up mismatched layers when it draws. Operations like `st_filter()` and `st_join()` won't, so transform first.

## Points on Polygons

```{r}
#| output-location: slide
#| fig-height: 5.5
#| out-width: "80%"
ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = state_lines, fill = "gray95", color = "gray50") +
  geom_sf(data = airports_ne, color = "#007155", size = 2) +
  coord_sf(crs = 5070) +
  theme_void() +
  labs(title = paste(nrow(airports_ne), "airports in the four NBRC states"),
       caption = "Source: nycflights13::airports; Census Bureau cartographic boundaries")
```

## Two Other Ways In {.smaller}

These two are made-up examples, so don't run them. There's no `grantees` shapefile or `clinics` table in your workspace.

**You have a shapefile.** A partner sends a `.zip`. Unzip it, keep all the pieces (`.shp`, `.shx`, `.dbf`, `.prj`) in one folder, and read the `.shp`:

```{r}
#| eval: false
grantees <- read_sf("data/grantees/grantees.shp")
```

**You only have addresses.** Turning addresses into coordinates is called **geocoding**. The `tidygeocoder` package can send them to the Census Bureau's free geocoder. It isn't in your workspace, so ask me if your team needs it.

```{r}
#| eval: false
library(tidygeocoder)
clinics_geo <- clinics |>
  geocode(address = full_address, method = "census")
```

# Spatial Joins {background-color="#007155"}

## Which Counties Are NBRC? {.smallest}

- NBRC doesn't serve every county in its four states. The list of the 63 it does serve is a small CSV on the course site.
- If you ran this last week, you already have `nbrc_fips`. Running it again is fine.

```{r}
#| eval: false
nbrc_fips <- read_csv(
  "https://andrewvanleuven.github.io/uvm_datasci/data/nbrc_counties_fips.csv",
  col_types = cols(.default = "c")
)
```

```{r}
nbrc_fips
```

- `full_fips` is the county's 5-digit FIPS code: 2 digits for the state, then 3 for the county. It's the same ID that `tigris` and `tidycensus` call `GEOID`.
- `col_types = cols(.default = "c")` reads every column as text, so `county_fips` keeps its leading zeros (`001`, not `1`)

## Which County Is Each Airport In?

- `airports` has no state or county column. The only "where" is the point itself.
- The county layer knows each county's name and state. Matching `GEOID` against `full_fips` adds whether it's in NBRC.

```{r}
nbrc_counties <- counties(state = nbrc_states, cb = TRUE) |>
  mutate(in_nbrc = GEOID %in% nbrc_fips$full_fips)

airports_joined <- airports_ne |>
  st_join(nbrc_counties)
```

- `GEOID %in% nbrc_fips$full_fips` is `TRUE` for the 63 NBRC counties and `FALSE` for the rest

## What `st_join()` Gave Us {.smaller}

```{r}
airports_joined |>
  select(name, NAME, STUSPS, in_nbrc)
```

- For each airport, `st_join()` found the county it sits in and copied that county's columns onto the airport's row
- It's a `left_join()` where the key is **location** instead of an ID. Same idea, same "keep every row on the left" behavior.

## Airports In and Out of NBRC Territory

```{r}
#| output-location: slide
#| fig-height: 5.5
#| out-width: "80%"
ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = nbrc_counties, fill = "gray95", color = "white") +
  geom_sf(data = state_lines, fill = NA, color = "gray50") +
  geom_sf(data = airports_joined, aes(color = in_nbrc), size = 2) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("TRUE" = "#007155", "FALSE" = "gray60"),
                     labels = c("TRUE" = "In an NBRC county", "FALSE" = "Outside NBRC"),
                     breaks = c("TRUE", "FALSE"), name = NULL) +
  coord_sf(crs = 5070) +
  theme_void() +
  theme(legend.position = "top")
```

## Going the Other Way: Points per Polygon {.smaller}

```{r}
airport_counts <- airports_joined |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  count(GEOID, name = "n_airports")

nbrc_airports <- nbrc_counties |>
  filter(in_nbrc) |>
  left_join(airport_counts, by = "GEOID") |>
  mutate(n_airports = replace_na(n_airports, 0))

nbrc_airports |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  count(n_airports)
```

- `st_drop_geometry()` turns the points back into a plain table, so `count()` is fast and the result joins by `GEOID` like any other table
- Counties with no airports don't show up in the count at all. `replace_na()` turns their missing value into a real zero.

## A Fact About the Region? or Just the Data? {.smaller}

```{r}
#| echo: false
no_airport <- sum(nbrc_airports$n_airports == 0)
vt_no_airport <- sum(nbrc_airports$n_airports == 0 & nbrc_airports$STUSPS == "VT")
```

- In this list, `r no_airport` of NBRC's 63 counties have no airport, including `r vt_no_airport` of Vermont's 14
- But the list isn't complete. It has `r sum(airports_joined$STUSPS == "VT")` Vermont airports and skips many small public airfields, including Newport State Airport in Orleans County.
- That's a fact about `nycflights13`, not about Vermont. It's fine for practice and wrong for a slide to NBRC.
- **Before you map a list of places, find out who made the list and what they left out**

## Spatial Join Cheat Sheet {.smaller}

| You want to... | Use |
|---|---|
| Turn lat/lon columns into points | `st_as_sf(coords = c("lon", "lat"), crs = 4326)` |
| Put two layers in the same CRS | `st_transform(x, st_crs(y))` |
| Keep only the points inside some polygons | `st_filter(points, polygons)` |
| Add each polygon's columns to the points in it | `st_join(points, polygons)` |
| Count points per polygon | `st_join()`, then `st_drop_geometry()`, `count()`, and `left_join()` |

: {tbl-colwidths="[45,55]"}

- That's the whole new skill set for tonight. Everything after the break is a tour.

# What Else Maps Can Do {background-color="#007155"}

## Watch, Don't Type

- The next few slides show maps your team might want for NBRC
- You won't be graded on any of them, and you don't need to follow along. The code is on the slides so you can come back to it.
- Each one builds on what you already know: `get_acs()`, `geom_sf()`, and tonight's points

## Dot Density: One Dot per 20 Households {.smaller}

```{r}
chittenden_tenure <- get_acs(
  geography = "block group",
  state = "VT",
  county = "Chittenden",
  variables = c(Owner = "B25003_002", Renter = "B25003_003"),
  year = 2024,
  geometry = TRUE
)

tenure_dots <- as_dot_density(
  chittenden_tenure,
  value = "estimate",
  values_per_dot = 20,
  group = "variable"
)
```

<!-- as_dot_density() runs in its own chunk on purpose: terra::dots() inside it keeps knitr from capturing a plot made in the same chunk. -->

```{r}
#| output-location: slide
#| fig-height: 5.5
#| out-width: "70%"
ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = chittenden_tenure, fill = "white", color = "gray85", linewidth = 0.1) +
  geom_sf(data = tenure_dots, aes(color = variable), size = 0.2) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c(Owner = "#1b9e77", Renter = "#d95f02"), name = NULL) +
  guides(color = guide_legend(override.aes = list(size = 3))) +
  theme_void() +
  labs(title = "Four in ten of Chittenden County's renter\nhouseholds live in the city of Burlington",
       caption = "One dot = 20 households, placed at random\nwithin its block group\nSource: 2020-2024 ACS 5-year estimates, table B25003")
```

## Dot Density {.smaller}

- `as_dot_density()` comes with `tidycensus`. It scatters dots at random inside each polygon, one per 20 households here.
- It shows **counts** without the "Chittenden wins every map" problem from last week, because empty land stays empty
- The dots are placed at random inside each block group. They aren't real addresses, so say so in the caption.
- Good for: two or three groups in one place (owners and renters, age groups, workers by industry)

## Proportional Symbols {.smaller}

```{r}
#| output-location: slide
#| fig-height: 5
#| out-width: "85%"
nbrc_renters <- get_acs(
  geography = "county",
  state = nbrc_states,
  variables = c(renters = "B25003_003", households = "B25003_001"),
  year = 2024,
  output = "wide",
  geometry = TRUE
) |>
  filter(GEOID %in% nbrc_fips$full_fips) |>
  mutate(renter_share = rentersE / householdsE)

renter_circles <- nbrc_renters |>
  st_point_on_surface()

ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = nbrc_renters, fill = "gray95", color = "white") +
  geom_sf(data = state_lines, fill = NA, color = "gray50") +
  geom_sf(data = renter_circles, aes(size = rentersE, fill = renter_share),
          shape = 21, color = "gray30", alpha = 0.9) +
  scale_size_area(max_size = 12, labels = scales::label_comma(),
                  name = "Renter\nhouseholds") +
  scale_fill_distiller(palette = "YlGnBu", direction = 1,
                       labels = scales::label_percent(), name = "Share\nrenting") +
  coord_sf(crs = 5070) +
  theme_void() +
  labs(title = "Six in ten of NBRC's renter households\nlive in its New York counties",
       caption = "Circle size: number of renter households. Color: share of households renting.\nSource: 2020-2024 ACS 5-year estimates, table B25003")
```

## Proportional Symbols {.smaller}

- Last week's rule: choropleths show rates, not counts. **Proportional symbols are where counts go.**
- `st_point_on_surface()` turns each county into one point inside it, and `aes(size = estimate)` scales the circle
- `scale_size_area()` makes a circle's *area*, not its width, proportional to the count. That's what eyes compare.
- Here the circle's **size** is the count and its **color** is the rate (`renters / households`), so one map shows both "how many" and "how common"

## Buffers: Who's Within 30 Miles? {.smaller}

```{r}
#| output-location: slide
#| fig-height: 5.5
#| out-width: "65%"
vt_towns <- county_subdivisions("VT", cb = TRUE) |>
  st_transform(5070)

btv <- airports_joined |>
  filter(faa == "BTV") |>
  st_transform(5070)

btv_buffer <- st_buffer(btv, dist = 30 * 1609.34)

vt_towns <- vt_towns |>
  mutate(near_btv = st_intersects(st_point_on_surface(vt_towns), btv_buffer,
                                  sparse = FALSE)[, 1])

ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = vt_towns, aes(fill = near_btv), color = "white", linewidth = 0.1) +
  geom_sf(data = btv_buffer, fill = NA, color = "black", linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_sf(data = btv, size = 3) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("TRUE" = "#007155", "FALSE" = "gray85"),
                    labels = c("TRUE" = "Within 30 miles", "FALSE" = "Farther"),
                    breaks = c("TRUE", "FALSE"), name = NULL) +
  theme_void() +
  labs(title = paste(sum(vt_towns$near_btv), "of Vermont's", nrow(vt_towns),
                     "towns are within\n30 miles of Burlington International"),
       caption = "Distance measured from each town's interior point, as the crow flies")
```

## Buffers and Distance {.smaller}

- `st_buffer()` draws a ring a set distance around each feature. Distance is in the CRS's units: meters for 5070, so 30 miles is `30 * 1609.34`.
- `st_intersects()` asks which towns fall inside the ring
- `st_distance()` gives the actual distance between features, and `st_nearest_feature()` finds the closest one
- **Rural Hub Services**: "how far is the nearest clinic, pharmacy, or grocery store?" is a buffer or distance question
- Straight-line distance understates a rural drive. Real drive times need a routing service, which is beyond this class.

## Interactive Maps with `mapgl` {.smaller}

```{r}
#| output-location: slide
#| echo: true
library(mapgl)

vt_home_value <- get_acs(
  geography = "tract",
  state = "VT",
  variables = c(home_value = "B25077_001"),
  year = 2024,
  geometry = TRUE
)

maplibre_view(vt_home_value, column = "estimate")
```

## Interactive Maps {.smaller}

- `mapgl` is already in your workspace. `maplibre_view()` is the one-line version: hand it an `sf` object and a column.
- Zoom, pan, and click a tract to see its value. The basemap underneath (roads, towns, water) is free.
- It drops straight into a **Quarto dashboard**, which is one of your two final-deliverable options
- Kyle Walker, who wrote `tidycensus` and the book you read for Week 9, also wrote `mapgl`. Its [documentation](https://walker-data.com/mapgl/) has many more examples.

# Finishing Touches {background-color="#007155"}

## Scale Bars and North Arrows {.smaller}

```{r}
#| output-location: slide
#| fig-height: 5.5
#| out-width: "65%"
library(ggspatial)

vt_seasonal <- get_acs(
  geography = "county subdivision",
  state = "VT",
  variables = c(seasonal = "B25004_006", units = "B25001_001"),
  year = 2024,
  output = "wide",
  geometry = TRUE
) |>
  mutate(seasonal_share = seasonalE / unitsE)

ggplot(vt_seasonal) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = seasonal_share), color = "white", linewidth = 0.1) +
  scale_fill_distiller(palette = "YlGnBu", direction = 1,
                       labels = scales::label_percent(), name = NULL,
                       na.value = "gray85") +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0.12, 0.02))) +
  annotation_scale(location = "bl", unit_category = "imperial") +
  annotation_north_arrow(location = "br", height = unit(1, "cm"),
                         width = unit(1, "cm"), style = north_arrow_minimal()) +
  theme_void() +
  labs(title = "In 51 Vermont towns, a third or more\nof homes are seasonal",
       caption = "Gray: no housing units\nSource: 2020-2024 ACS 5-year estimates, tables B25004 and B25001")
```

## Do You Need Them? {.smaller}

- `annotation_scale()` and `annotation_north_arrow()` come from `ggspatial`, which is already in your workspace
- `location = "bl"` means bottom left, and `"br"` is bottom right. Put them where they won't cover the data. `unit_category = "imperial"` gives miles.
- `scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0.12, 0.02)))` adds a little empty space below the map (12% of its height) so the scale bar doesn't sit on the towns
- **Scale bar**: worth it whenever distance matters to the story (access, commuting, service areas). It's required on HW5.
- **North arrow**: optional. On a map of a familiar place with north at the top, most cartographers leave it off. Never let it compete with the data.

## Inset Maps: Where Is This? {.smaller}

```{r}
#| output-location: slide
#| fig-height: 5.5
#| out-width: "70%"
library(patchwork)

locator <- ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = state_lines, aes(fill = STUSPS == "VT"), color = "white") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("TRUE" = "#007155", "FALSE" = "gray80"), guide = "none") +
  coord_sf(crs = 5070) +
  ggplot2::theme_void() +
  theme(plot.background = element_rect(fill = "white", color = "gray50"))

seasonal_map <- ggplot(vt_seasonal) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = seasonal_share), color = "white", linewidth = 0.1) +
  scale_fill_distiller(palette = "YlGnBu", direction = 1,
                       labels = scales::label_percent(), name = NULL,
                       na.value = "gray85") +
  theme_void()

seasonal_map +
  inset_element(locator, left = 0.62, bottom = 0.05, right = 0.95, top = 0.35,
                align_to = "full")
```

## Inset Maps {.smaller}

- A **locator inset** tells an outside reader where the main map sits. NBRC staff know where Vermont is, but a federal reviewer reading their report might not know where Essex County is.
- `inset_element()` comes from the `patchwork` package, which is **not** in your workspace. Install it with `install.packages("patchwork")` if your team wants one.
- The positions (`left`, `bottom`, `right`, `top`) run from 0 to 1 across the whole figure (`align_to = "full"`). Expect to nudge them a few times.

## A Finished-Map Checklist {.smaller}

- [ ] A **title that states the finding**, not just the variable
- [ ] A **source caption** naming the data and the table or dataset
- [ ] **Rates, shares, or medians** on a choropleth; counts as dots or symbols
- [ ] A **readable palette**, with missing data in gray and labeled as missing
- [ ] **Formatted legend labels**: `label_percent()`, `label_dollar()`, `label_comma()`
- [ ] **A sensible CRS**: 5070 for a multi-state map
- [ ] **`theme_void()`**: no latitude and longitude grid
- [ ] A **scale bar** when distance matters
- [ ] **Small-area caution**: check margins of error before you claim two places differ

# Git, GitHub, and HW5 {background-color="#007155"}

## What Are Git and GitHub? {.smaller}

- **Git** keeps a history of a project. Each saved snapshot is a **commit**, so you can see what changed, when, and go back if you need to.
- **GitHub** is a website that hosts git projects so other people can download them, use them, and suggest changes
- You've already used both. Every homework you've pulled with `git fetch && git checkout ...` came from my GitHub repository.
- Many R packages live on GitHub, often a newer version than the one on CRAN (where `install.packages()` looks), and sometimes *only* on GitHub
- Your team could use GitHub to share code for the final deliverable. Ask me if you want help setting that up.

## Installing a Package from GitHub {.smaller}

- `install.packages()` only searches CRAN. For GitHub, use the `remotes` package. Run these **once**, in the **Console**:

```{r}
#| eval: false
install.packages("remotes")
remotes::install_github("UrbanInstitute/education-data-package-r",
                        upgrade = "never")
```

- `upgrade = "never"` stops it from asking whether to update every other package you have
- The first argument is `"owner/repository"`, copied from the GitHub address: [github.com/UrbanInstitute/education-data-package-r](https://github.com/UrbanInstitute/education-data-package-r)
- The repository name and the package name can differ. This one installs a package called `educationdata`, so you'll load it with `library(educationdata)`.
- Installing from GitHub runs someone else's code on your computer. Stick to sources you trust, like a university, a research institute, or a package author you know.

::: {.notes}
educationdata is also on CRAN, but the point tonight is the GitHub workflow, and the GitHub version is the newest.
:::

## Colleges as Points {.smaller}

```{r}
vt_colleges <- get_education_data(
  level = "college-university",
  source = "ipeds",
  topic = "directory",
  filters = list(year = 2024, fips = 50)
)

vt_colleges |>
  select(inst_name, city, latitude, longitude) |>
  head()
```

- The Urban Institute's Education Data Portal serves federal **IPEDS** data on every college and university. `fips = 50` is Vermont's state FIPS code.
- It has `latitude` and `longitude` columns, so you already know the next step. That's HW5, Part 2.
